introduction-marketing-vs-reality.core: Database vendors advertise guarantees such as 'strongly consistent', 'ACID' and 'linearizable', but those claims are rarely tested under partitions, clock skew and crashes. Jepsen, created by Kyle Kingsbury, puts a system under realistic faults, records every operation, and checks whether the history actually satisfies the claimed consistency model. It has found violations in most systems it has tested.

first_principles.problem: A team picks a database for 'strong consistency' and later loses acknowledged writes during a network partition.
truths: Claims are often untested under faults.

analogy.title: Crash-testing cars instead of reading brochures
analogy.story: The brochure says 'safe'; the crash test shows what happens at 60 km/h into a wall.
analogy.breaks: Cars crash once; Jepsen replays many random fault schedules.

check.q: Why test consistency under faults specifically?
check.a: Most systems behave correctly when healthy; guarantees only matter, and most often break, during partitions, crashes and clock problems.

how-jepsen-works-the-architecture.core: Jepsen is a Clojure framework: a control node SSHes into (typically) five database nodes to install and start the system. Client processes run a workload, generating operations such as reads, writes and compare-and-sets, and each records invoke and complete events with timestamps. A nemesis process injects faults concurrently, and a checker analyses the full history afterwards.

first_principles.problem: Engineers want to test their own system Jepsen-style but don't understand its parts.
truths: Every op needs invoke and completion.

analogy.title: A lab experiment
analogy.story: A technician sets up equipment, a script feeds samples, a saboteur shakes the bench, and an analyst reviews the logbook.
analogy.breaks: Lab results are measurements; Jepsen results are proofs of violation.

example.title: Test definition

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 120 s of mixed ops with partitions every 5 s, then a linearizability check.

code.text:
(defn my-test [opts]
  (merge tests/noop-test opts
    {:name      "mydb-register"
     :db        (db "1.4.2")
     :client    (->RegisterClient nil)
     :nemesis   (nemesis/partition-random-halves)
     :generator (->> (gen/mix [r w cas])
                     (gen/nemesis (cycle [(gen/sleep 5) {:f :start} (gen/sleep 5) {:f :stop}]))
                     (gen/time-limit 120))
     :checker   (checker/linearizable {:model (model/cas-register)})}))

example.outcome: the moving parts of a Jepsen test.

check.q: What does an ':info' completion mean in a Jepsen history?
check.a: The outcome is indeterminate (for example a timeout); the op may or may not have taken effect, so the checker must consider both.

the-nemesis-chaos-on-demand.core: The nemesis is Jepsen's fault injector. It partitions networks with iptables (random halves, isolate the primary, bridges, rings), kills or pauses processes with SIGKILL and SIGSTOP, skews or strobes clocks, and can corrupt or truncate files. Faults are scheduled alongside client operations so the system is exercised while it is degraded and while it recovers.

first_principles.problem: Tests that only kill nodes never trigger the asymmetric partition that causes split-brain.
truths: Recovery is as risky as failure.

analogy.title: A fire drill run by a mischievous examiner
analogy.story: They block different exits, cut power and fake alarms at random times to see if procedures really work.
analogy.breaks: Drills are announced; nemesis faults hit mid-operation.

example.title: Bridge partition
flow: Both sides can form 'majorities' with n3
Two leaders may emerge if quorum logic is wrong

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Exposes bugs that clean splits never trigger.

check.q: Why is a SIGSTOP pause more dangerous than a SIGKILL?
check.a: A paused process resumes believing its state and leases are still valid, potentially acting as a stale leader; a killed one restarts cleanly.

the-analysis-linearizability-checking.core: After the run, the checker asks: is there any order of operations, consistent with real-time (an op that completed before another began must come first) and with the data type's semantics, that explains every observed result? Knossos searches that space for linearizability (NP-complete in general, so histories are kept small), while Elle infers dependency cycles in transactional histories to detect serializability anomalies such as G2 and lost updates.

first_principles.problem: A reviewer can't tell whether an odd read is a bug or just concurrency.
truths: Concurrent ops can linearize in many orders.
No valid order means a violation.

analogy.title: A detective reconstructing a timeline
analogy.story: Given witness statements with time windows, is there any sequence of events consistent with all of them? If not, someone's story is impossible.
analogy.breaks: Witnesses lie; histories are precise but timeouts leave ambiguity.

example.title: Non-linearizable history
flow: B: read starts at t=3, returns 0
Real time says write(1) precedes read
No legal order → stale read violation

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Proof that the system served stale data.

check.q: Why does Jepsen keep linearizability histories short?
check.a: Checking linearizability is NP-complete in general, so search cost explodes with history length and concurrency.

real-world-findings-what-jepsen-actually.core: Jepsen analyses have found lost acknowledged writes in early MongoDB and Elasticsearch, split-brain in Redis Sentinel, stale reads in etcd and Consul before their linearizable-read fixes, serializability violations in several SQL and NewSQL databases, and misleading documentation almost everywhere. Vendors typically fix the bugs and correct the docs, and many now run Jepsen in CI.

first_principles.problem: A team assumes mature, popular databases must already be correct under partitions.
derivation: Read the **Jepsen report** for your DB and version.
Check which **settings** were needed for safety.
Prefer **safe defaults** (majority write concern, linearizable reads).
Add **Jepsen-style tests** to your own CI.

analogy.title: Food inspection reports
analogy.story: Even famous restaurants fail inspections; the report tells you what was wrong and whether it was fixed.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants are re-inspected yearly; DB versions change behaviour with each release.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Avoids the rollback-of-acknowledged-writes class of bugs.

check.q: What practical step should you take after reading a Jepsen report for your database?
check.a: Check which version and settings were tested, adopt the safe configuration (e.g. majority writes/reads), and verify after upgrades.
